Title: Tranzakt Finance
Outcome Line: One login for 30+ Nigerian bank accounts, and the 268-variant design system that keeps it coherent across eight product surfaces.
Outcome Result: [Add a business result here when available, e.g. onboarding time, adoption, support tickets]
Context: Nigerian businesses run money across several banks — GTBank, Zenith, Access, UBA, FCMB and more — each with its own login, its own dashboard and its own idea of a balance. Tranzakt's promise is simple: one screen, all accounts, one login, at SME-grade pricing with enterprise-grade access control.
Problem: Eight products were being designed in parallel. Without a shared system, every surface would drift: competing greens, a growing font stack, and a new button for every screen. The real problem wasn't any single flow. It was keeping the whole platform coherent while it was still being invented.
Scope:
• KYC/KYB onboarding
  • Treasury management
  • Wallet & Payout
  • Payment Gateway checkout
  • Tranzpay Transfer
  • Merchant AI
  • Admin Analytics
  • Marketing website & Careers
Section 1 Heading: A design system built to stop variant explosion
Section 1 Summary: 33 components and 268 variants across atoms, molecules and organisms — structured so the system grows by composition, not by duplication.
Section 1 Body: Instead of giant variant matrices, components are assembled from small building-block sub-components. A button doesn't get a variant for every icon and size combination; it gets slots. Spacing runs on an 8pt system. Type follows one rule: labels and headers in Outfit, anything a person reads or types in Avenir. One icon library — Vuesax — and nothing hand-drawn. Responsive versions reflow with real auto-layout; scaled-down desktop frames were rejected outright.
Section 1 Decisions:
• Building-block sub-components over variant matrices
  • 8pt spacing system across every surface
  • Outfit for labels, Avenir for read and typed text
  • Responsive = real reflow, never scaled frames
Section 2 Heading: A checkout that only shows the fee you'll actually pay
Section 2 Summary: Card, Transfer, USSD and Bank — identical on web and mobile, with fees revealed only for the method you choose.
Section 2 Body: Customers see the base amount until they pick a method. Then a small info icon opens a breakdown of that one transaction: base amount plus that channel's fee. No intimidating table of every channel's charges up front. The copy button beside the amount appears only on USSD and Transfer — the two methods where people genuinely need to copy a number into another app.
Section 2 Decisions:
• Base amount first; fee revealed per chosen method
  • Tooltip shows the current transaction only
  • Copy affordance only where copying happens
  • Four methods, matched across web and mobile
Section 3 Heading: One verification module for every product and user type
Section 3 Summary: KYC/KYB for Personal, Business and Government users — six sections, every state mapped, one module shared across the platform.
Section 3 Body: The verification module serves every Tranzakt product, so its copy never names one. Six onboarding sections specify Nigerian compliance data — BVN, NIN, CAC, SCUML — field by field. Progress-tracking widgets were removed to cut clutter, and failed documents get one clear message rather than per-document admin notes, which keeps review scalable. Each user type is mapped through success, failed submission, in review, action required, edge cases, and save & quit. Mobile uses exactly the same fields as web.
Section 3 Decisions:
• One generic module serving every product
  • Tracking widgets removed
  • One clear failure message, not per-document notes
  • Mobile fields identical to web
Section 4 Summary: Five AI pillars for merchants under one interaction model — and a rule that every insight must come with a decision.
Section 4 Body: Onboarding, natural-language payment setup, tracking and insights, forecasting, and collections all follow one pattern: the AI explains what's happening, recommends what to do, and executes only when the merchant agrees. Actionable items sit above analytics; no decorative data without a decision attached. The direction is backed by a pattern study of Stripe, Mercury, Ramp, Cleo, Intuit, Lorikeet and Revolut.
Section 4 Decisions:
• Explain → Recommend → Execute, every time
  • Actions above analytics
  • No decorative data
  • Grounded in a 7-product pattern study
